q: You (blue car) and the red car reach this all-way stop at the same moment. The red car is on your right. Who goes first?
options: You go first because you are going straight
Whoever honks first
The red car goes first
explain: When two drivers arrive at an all-way stop together, the driver on the left yields to the driver on the right, so the red car has the right-of-way.

q: At an intersection with no signs or signals, another car has already entered the intersection from a cross street when you arrive. What should you do?
options: Yield to the car that is already in the intersection
Go first if you are on the wider street
Go first if the other car is on your left
explain: A driver approaching an intersection must yield to any vehicle that has already entered it from a different road.

q: You are on a road that ends at a T-intersection with a through road. There are no signs or signals. A car on the through road arrives at the same time as you. Who must yield?
options: The driver on the through road
Whichever driver is on the left
You, because your road ends there
explain: At an uncontrolled intersection, a driver on a road that ends (does not continue past the intersection) must yield to traffic on the road that continues.

q: You approach an intersection where the traffic lights are not working at all (completely dark). What must you do?
options: Stop, then go only when it is safe to do so
Slow down and continue if no one is coming
Keep the same speed because you have no signal to obey
explain: When signals are inoperative, every driver must stop at the intersection and may proceed with caution only when it is safe.

q: You (blue car) want to turn left on a green light. The red car is coming toward you and going straight. What should you do?
options: Wait and let the red car pass before turning
Turn quickly before the red car gets close
Turn because a green light gives you the right-of-way
explain: A driver turning left must yield to oncoming vehicles that are close enough to be a hazard and keep yielding until the turn can be made safely.

q: You are about to turn left from a street into a private driveway. An oncoming car is close enough to be a hazard. What does the law require?
options: You may turn because you signaled first
The oncoming car must stop for you
You must yield to the oncoming car until it is safe to turn
explain: The left-turn yield rule also applies when turning into public or private property or an alley: oncoming traffic that is a hazard goes first.

q: You stop at a stop sign where cross traffic does not have to stop. After stopping, when may you enter the intersection?
options: Right after stopping, because cross traffic must yield to you
When no vehicle on the cross street is close enough to be an immediate hazard
Only after waiting at least 10 seconds
explain: After stopping, a driver must yield to cross traffic that is approaching closely enough to be an immediate hazard, then may proceed when it is reasonably safe.

q: You arrive at an intersection controlled by this sign. What must you do?
options: Come to a full stop every time, even if the road is clear
Speed up to merge ahead of cross traffic
Slow down and give the right-of-way to vehicles in or close to the intersection, stopping if needed
explain: At a yield sign you must give the right-of-way to vehicles already in the intersection or close enough to be an immediate hazard; you stop only when necessary.

q: You are pulling out of a shopping center parking lot onto a public street. Who has the right-of-way?
options: Traffic on the street that is close enough to be a hazard
You do, once your front bumper is in the street
Whoever is driving the larger vehicle
explain: A driver entering a street from private property or an alley must yield to all approaching traffic close enough to be an immediate hazard.

q: Before you drive across a sidewalk to leave a driveway, a person is walking toward your path on the sidewalk. What should you do?
options: Yield to the person walking on the sidewalk
Honk so the person knows to stop
Drive across quickly before the person arrives
explain: Before driving over a sidewalk, a driver must yield to any pedestrian approaching on it.

q: A pedestrian is crossing in the crosswalk ahead of you (blue car). What must you do?
options: Drive around the pedestrian if there is room
Yield and let the pedestrian finish crossing safely
Honk so the pedestrian hurries
explain: Drivers must yield to pedestrians crossing in a marked crosswalk and must slow down or take other action as needed to keep them safe.

q: A pedestrian is crossing at a street corner where there are no painted crosswalk lines. Must you yield?
options: No, pedestrians only have the right-of-way in painted crosswalks
Only if a traffic signal is present
Yes, a corner crossing is an unmarked crosswalk and you must yield
explain: The duty to yield covers pedestrians in marked crosswalks and in unmarked crosswalks at intersections.

q: A car in the lane next to you has stopped at a crosswalk to let a pedestrian cross. What should you do?
options: Pass the stopped car carefully
Change lanes behind it and then pass
Do not pass the stopped car; stop and wait
explain: When a vehicle has stopped at a crosswalk for a pedestrian, drivers coming from behind may not pass it, because the pedestrian may be hidden from view.

q: A pedestrian is crossing in the middle of a block, away from any crosswalk. Which statement is correct?
options: The pedestrian should yield to nearby vehicles, but you must still use care to avoid hitting them
You may keep going at the same speed because the pedestrian is breaking the rule
The pedestrian always has the right-of-way, so you must stop in any lane
explain: Outside a crosswalk a pedestrian must yield to vehicles close enough to be a hazard, but that does not remove a driver's duty to use due care for the pedestrian's safety.

q: A pedestrian using a guide dog, or carrying a white cane (with or without a red tip), is about to cross in front of you. What must you do?
options: Give the pedestrian the right-of-way and take every needed precaution
Honk to warn the pedestrian
Drive past slowly, since the pedestrian cannot see you
explain: California gives blind or partially blind pedestrians with a white cane or guide dog the right-of-way, and failing to yield to them is a misdemeanor.

q: In California, failing to yield to a blind pedestrian who uses a white cane or guide dog is a misdemeanor with a fine of at least $___.
explain: The law sets a fine of $500 to $1,000, jail of up to six months, or both, for failing to yield to a blind pedestrian.

q: You stopped at a red light and want to turn right, and no sign prohibits it. Who must you yield to before turning?
options: Pedestrians in the nearby crosswalk and vehicles close enough to be a hazard
Only vehicles turning left from the opposite direction
No one, because a right turn on red is always allowed
explain: After stopping, a right turn on red is allowed only while yielding to pedestrians in the adjacent crosswalk and to vehicles close enough to be an immediate hazard.

q: Your light turns green, but a pedestrian is still in the crosswalk in front of you. What should you do?
options: Go, since the green light gives you the right-of-way
Wait until the pedestrian has crossed
Inch forward to signal the pedestrian to hurry
explain: Even on a green light, drivers must yield to pedestrians and vehicles that are lawfully within the intersection or an adjacent crosswalk.

q: Your light is green, but traffic is backed up on the far side of the intersection and there is no room for your car. What should you do?
options: Enter and wait in the intersection until traffic moves
Enter only if you are turning
Wait behind the intersection until there is space for your car on the other side
explain: California's anti-gridlock law forbids entering an intersection, even on green, unless there is room on the other side so you will not block cross traffic.

q: Traffic ahead is stopped. Where should you avoid coming to a stop?
options: In a position that blocks a crosswalk
Behind the white stop line
A safe distance behind the car ahead
explain: It is illegal to stop a vehicle unnecessarily in a way that blocks a marked or unmarked crosswalk or a sidewalk.

q: An ambulance with its siren on and red lights flashing comes up behind you (blue car). What must you do?
options: Speed up to stay ahead of it
Stop right where you are in your lane
Drive to the right edge of the road and stop until it passes
explain: When an emergency vehicle approaches with a siren and red light, drivers must yield, move to the right-hand edge or curb, stop, and stay stopped until it passes.

q: You are in the middle of an intersection when you hear a siren and see a fire truck with red lights coming. What should you do?
options: Stop immediately inside the intersection
Back up out of the intersection
Continue through the intersection, then pull to the right and stop
explain: The law says to pull to the right edge and stop clear of any intersection, so finish crossing first and then pull over.

q: You are driving in a carpool (HOV) lane when an emergency vehicle with a siren and red light approaches. What should you do?
options: Stay in the carpool lane and slow down
Stop in the carpool lane
Leave the carpool lane as soon as you can do so safely
explain: A driver in an exclusive or preferential use lane must exit that lane as soon as it can be done with reasonable safety when an emergency vehicle approaches.

q: Unless you are driving an emergency vehicle, you may not follow a fire truck or ambulance that is responding to an emergency within ___ feet.
explain: California forbids following within 300 feet of an emergency vehicle that is responding to an emergency.

q: A police car with flashing lights is stopped on the right shoulder. You (blue car) are in the right lane of a multi-lane road. What should you do if the next lane is clear?
options: Move over one lane, away from the police car, when it is safe
Stay in your lane and keep your speed
Stop next to the police car
explain: California's move-over law tells drivers to change into a lane not next to a stopped emergency vehicle when that is safe and practical.

q: You are approaching a tow truck with flashing amber lights stopped on the shoulder, but heavy traffic makes changing lanes unsafe. What should you do?
options: Stay in your lane and slow to a safe speed while passing
Stop in your lane until the tow truck leaves
Pass on the shoulder on the other side
explain: If moving over is unsafe or impractical, the move-over law requires you to slow to a reasonable and prudent speed for the conditions.

q: As of January 1, 2026, California's move-over law also covers which of these stopped vehicles?
options: Any parked car with no lights on
Vehicles in a parking lot separated from the road by a barrier
Any stopped vehicle on the roadside showing hazard lights, cones, or flares
explain: The law was expanded to include any stationary vehicle displaying hazard lights or warning devices such as cones, flares, or reflectors; it does not apply where a physical barrier separates the vehicle from the road.

q: The school bus ahead of you (blue car) is stopped with red lights flashing and its stop arm out. What must you do?
options: Pass slowly on the left
Stop and stay stopped until the red lights stop flashing
Stop, then go once you see no children
explain: Drivers must stop before passing a school bus that shows flashing red lights and a stop arm, and may not move past it until those signals turn off.

q: You are on a divided highway. A school bus with flashing red lights is stopped on the other roadway, across the median. Must you stop?
options: No, you do not need to stop
Yes, all traffic must stop
Only if children are crossing toward you
explain: On a divided highway, or a road with two or more lanes in each direction, you need not stop for a school bus on the other roadway.

q: On a two-lane road, an oncoming school bus stops in front of you with red lights flashing and the stop arm out. What must you do?
options: Keep going, since the bus is in the other lane
Slow to 25 mph and pass
Stop until the red lights stop flashing
explain: The school bus stop rule applies to drivers meeting the bus from either direction unless the road is divided or has two or more lanes each way.

q: A school bus ahead of you turns on its flashing amber (yellow) lights. What does this usually mean?
options: The bus is about to stop to load or unload students
The bus is turning right
You may pass the bus quickly
explain: School bus drivers turn on the amber warning lights as they approach a stop, beginning 200 feet before it, so expect the bus to stop and the red lights to come on.

q: The railroad crossing gates are down and the lights are flashing. You (blue car) see no train yet. What should you do?
options: Drive around the gates carefully if no train is visible
Back up and cross at a different angle
Stay stopped until the gates go up and it is safe
explain: It is illegal to drive through, around, or under a railroad crossing gate while it is closed.

q: When a railroad crossing signal warns that a train is coming, you must stop at least ___ feet from the nearest rail.
explain: Drivers must stop no closer than 15 feet from the nearest rail when a signal, flagger, or nearby train warns of danger.

q: Traffic is slow on the far side of a railroad crossing. When may you start across the tracks?
options: Only when there is room on the other side for your whole vehicle
As soon as the signals are off, even if you might stop on the tracks
Whenever the car ahead of you starts across
explain: You may not enter a rail crossing, even with a signal to proceed, unless there is enough space on the other side for your vehicle.

q: You are following a bus carrying passengers toward a railroad crossing with no train in sight. What should you expect?
options: The bus will speed up to cross quickly
The bus will stop before the tracks even if no train is coming
The bus will stop only if the gates are down
explain: Buses carrying passengers, school buses with students, and trucks carrying certain hazardous materials generally must stop before the tracks and look and listen for trains.

q: Buses carrying passengers must stop at railroad crossings no less than 15 feet and no more than ___ feet from the nearest rail.
explain: These vehicles must stop between 15 and 50 feet from the nearest rail and look and listen in both directions before crossing.

q: You (blue car) are at the yield line about to enter this roundabout. Who has the right-of-way?
options: Vehicles already circling in the roundabout
You, because you are entering
Whoever is on the right
explain: Roundabouts use yield control at entry: vehicles already on the circular roadway may proceed, and entering drivers wait for a safe gap.

q: In a roundabout in the United States, which direction does traffic travel around the center island?
options: Clockwise
Either direction, whichever is shorter
Counterclockwise
explain: Traffic in a roundabout circulates counterclockwise, passing to the right of the center island.

q: A funeral procession is being escorted by a uniformed peace officer who signals you to wait. What should you do?
options: Obey the officer and wait
Follow your green light instead of the officer
Join the end of the procession to get through
explain: Ignoring the direction of a uniformed peace officer escorting a funeral procession is an infraction in California.

q: On a steep, narrow mountain road, two cars meet and there is not enough room to pass. Which driver must yield?
options: The driver going uphill
The driver of the smaller car
The driver going downhill
explain: When a grade is too narrow for vehicles to pass, the driver going downhill must yield and, if necessary, back up to a place where passing is possible.

q: You see these lines in the center of a two-lane road. May you cross them to pass a slow car?
options: Yes, if no traffic is coming
Only during daylight hours
No, you may not drive to the left of these lines to pass
explain: Double solid yellow lines prohibit driving to the left of them to pass in either direction.

q: With these center lines, when may you cross them?
options: To pass a slow vehicle
Never, under any circumstances
To turn left into a driveway or at an intersection
explain: Double yellow lines may be crossed to turn left at an intersection or into or out of a driveway or private road, or for a legal U-turn, but not to pass.

q: Your car is in the lower-right lane. The solid yellow line is on your side of the center. May you pass the car ahead by crossing the center line?
options: No, passing is not allowed from your side
Yes, if the road ahead is clear
Yes, but only to pass a bicycle
explain: When a solid and a broken yellow line are side by side, only drivers on the broken-line side may cross to pass; a solid line on your side means no passing.

q: Your car is in the lower-right lane, and the broken yellow line is on your side of the center. What do these lines allow?
options: You may pass when the way ahead is clear and safe
Nothing; they mean no passing in both directions
Only oncoming traffic may pass
explain: A driver on the side with the broken line may cross the double line to overtake and pass when it is safe.

q: What does a single broken yellow center line on a two-lane road mean?
options: Traffic in both lanes moves the same direction
Passing is never allowed
Traffic moves in opposite directions, and passing with care is allowed in either direction when safe
explain: A single broken yellow center line separates opposing traffic and marks a zone where drivers in either direction may pass with care.

q: What does the broken white line between these two lanes mean?
options: Both lanes go the same direction, and you may change lanes when it is safe
The lanes carry traffic in opposite directions
You may never change lanes here
explain: Broken white lane lines separate lanes moving in the same direction where crossing with care is allowed.

q: Two lanes going the same direction are separated by a solid white line. What does this tell you?
options: Lane changes are encouraged here
Changing lanes across this line is discouraged
The left lane is for oncoming traffic
explain: A solid white lane line is used where crossing between same-direction lanes is discouraged, such as near intersections and turn lanes.

q: What is the center lane marked like this used for?
options: Passing slow traffic
Parking during rush hour
Left turns (and legal U-turns) by drivers from both directions
explain: A two-way left-turn lane is set aside for vehicles making left turns in both directions; it is outlined by a solid outer and a broken inner yellow line.

q: Traffic in your lane is moving slowly. May you drive in this center lane to get past it?
options: Yes, if the lane is empty
Yes, for up to half a mile
No, this lane is only for preparing to turn left or make a legal U-turn
explain: A two-way left-turn lane may be used only when preparing for or making a left turn or legal U-turn, not for passing or through travel.

q: The left lane is marked with white diamond symbols. What does this mean?
options: It is a high-occupancy vehicle (carpool) lane; follow the posted occupancy rules
It is a lane for trucks only
It is an emergency stopping lane
explain: A white diamond marks a high-occupancy vehicle (HOV) lane, and drivers may use it only as allowed by the posted signs.

q: On this divided road, what does the solid yellow line along the left side of your lanes mark?
options: A lane for oncoming traffic
A bike lane
The left edge of the roadway
explain: On divided highways and one-way roads, a solid yellow line marks the left edge of the roadway; the right edge is marked in white.

q: You must stop for a red light at this intersection. Where should you stop?
options: Behind the white stop line
In the crosswalk
Past the crosswalk, at the edge of the cross street
explain: On a steady red signal, stop at the marked limit (stop) line, or before the crosswalk if there is no line.

q: Which color of center line separates traffic moving in opposite directions?
explain: Yellow lines separate traffic going in opposite directions; white lines separate lanes going the same way.

q: What do double solid white lines between lanes mean?
options: You may cross them with care
You must not cross them
They mark the edge of a parking area
explain: California law forbids crossing any part of double parallel solid white lines except in limited cases.

q: A carpool (HOV) lane is separated from the other lanes by double solid lines. How may you enter or leave it?
options: Anywhere, as long as you signal
Only by crossing the lines at an exit ramp
Only at places marked for entry and exit, such as where a single broken line is used
explain: You may not cross double solid lines next to an HOV lane; enter or exit only in designated areas or where a single broken line is in place.

q: You may not drive in a two-way left-turn lane for more than ___ feet while preparing for and making a turn.
explain: California limits travel in a two-way left-turn lane to 200 feet while preparing for and making the turn or merging out.

q: Your turn signal must be on continuously during the last ___ feet before you turn.
explain: A signal of intent to turn must be given continuously for the last 100 feet before the turn.

q: You are giving a hand signal from the driver's window. Your arm is held straight out to the side. What does this mean?
options: Left turn
Right turn
Slowing or stopping
explain: A hand and arm extended horizontally out of the left side of the vehicle signals a left turn.

q: Which hand signal means you plan to turn right?
options: Left arm bent upward at the elbow
Left arm pointing straight down
Left arm straight out to the side
explain: A right turn is signaled with the hand and arm extended upward outside the left side of the vehicle.

q: Which hand signal tells drivers behind you that you are stopping or slowing suddenly?
options: Left arm straight out to the side
Left arm bent upward
Left arm extended downward
explain: A hand and arm extended downward outside the vehicle signals a stop or sudden decrease in speed.

q: Your turn signals stop working while you are driving. What does the law require when you need to signal?
options: Use hand and arm signals
Flash your headlights
Turn on your hazard lights before each turn
explain: If signal lamps become inoperable while driving, the driver must use hand and arm signals instead.

q: How should you make a right turn?
options: Swing wide into the left lane first
Start and finish the turn as close as practical to the right curb or edge
Turn from the center of the road
explain: Both the approach and the right turn itself should be made as close as practicable to the right-hand curb or edge of the road.

q: How should you make a left turn at an intersection on a two-way street?
options: Approach from the far-left lane, start turning inside the intersection, and finish in a legal lane
Start turning before you reach the intersection to save time
Approach from the right lane so you can see better
explain: A left turn is approached from the far-left lawful lane, is not begun before entering the intersection, and must end in a lane open to your direction.

q: You (blue car) want to turn right at the next corner, and a marked bike lane runs along the curb. What should you do?
options: Turn from your lane, crossing the bike lane at the corner
Wait until the cyclist is beside you, then turn
When it is safe, signal and move into the bike lane before turning
explain: When you must cross an adjacent bike lane to turn, you should move into the bike lane before the turn, after checking that it is safe and signaling.

q: You may drive in a bike lane to prepare for a turn only within ___ feet of the intersection.
explain: Motor vehicles may use a bike lane to prepare for a turn only within 200 feet of the intersection, or to park or to enter or leave the road.

q: When is passing another vehicle on the right allowed?
options: Any time you are in a hurry, using the shoulder
Never, under any circumstances
When the car ahead is turning left and there is room on the paved road
explain: Passing on the right is allowed in limited cases, such as when the vehicle ahead is turning left, and never by driving off the paved roadway.

q: On a two-lane road, you may not drive on the left side of the road to pass within ___ feet of an intersection or railroad crossing.
explain: Driving on the left side of the road is not allowed within 100 feet of, or while crossing, an intersection or railroad grade crossing.

q: Another driver is passing you on the left. What should you do?
options: Speed up so they finish passing quickly
Move left to block them
Keep to the right and do not speed up until they have passed
explain: A driver being overtaken must move safely to the right and must not increase speed until the passing vehicle has fully passed.

q: On a two-lane road where passing is unsafe, a slow vehicle with ___ or more vehicles lined up behind it must pull off at the nearest turnout or safe area.
explain: A slow driver with five or more vehicles in line behind must use the nearest turnout or safe area to let them pass.

q: In a business district, where may you make a U-turn?
options: At an intersection, or through an opening provided in a divided highway
Anywhere if no cars are coming
In the middle of the block
explain: In a business district, U-turns are allowed only at intersections or at designated openings in a divided highway.

q: In a residence district, you may not make a U-turn when another vehicle is approaching within 200 feet, unless:
options: You are at an intersection where a signal or sign controls the approaching vehicle
You signal first
You complete the turn quickly
explain: A residential U-turn is not allowed with a vehicle approaching within 200 feet, except at an intersection where a traffic control device controls that vehicle.

q: You want to make a U-turn at an intersection with a traffic light and no sign prohibiting it. Which lane must you turn from?
options: The right lane
Any lane, as long as you signal
The far-left lane available to your direction of travel
explain: At a signal-controlled intersection, a U-turn may be made only from the far-left lane lawfully available to your direction of travel.

q: You (blue car) are on the on-ramp and about to merge onto the freeway. What should you do?
options: Merge immediately; freeway traffic must make room for you
Signal and move into a freeway lane only when there is a safe gap
Stop at the end of the ramp and back up if no gap appears
explain: You may change lanes only when it can be done with reasonable safety and after signaling, so look for a safe gap before merging.

q: A freeway on-ramp has a traffic signal (ramp meter) showing red. What must you do?
options: Stop at the limit line and wait for green
Merge carefully without stopping
Ignore it if the freeway looks clear
explain: Traffic signals at places other than intersections, including freeway on-ramps, must be obeyed; stop at the marked line or sign.
